This is an empty module — it contains no code, no imports, and no definitions [[target/app/api/__init__.py]]. Its sole role is to mark the `app/api` directory as a Python package, making it importable by other parts of the application [[target/app/api/__init__.py]].

This is an empty module file that serves as a package initializer for the `app/api/dependencies` package, containing no definitions, imports, or logic of its own [[target/app/api/dependencies/__init__.py]].

`check_article_modification_permissions` is a FastAPI dependency function that enforces write-access control on an article, returning nothing on success and blocking the request if the current user is not permitted to modify the article [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::check_article_modification_permissions]].

It accepts two injected parameters: `current_article`, an `Article` instance resolved via the `get_article_by_slug_from_path` dependency, and `user`, a `User` instance resolved via `get_current_user_authorizer()` [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::get_article_by_slug_from_path]] [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::get_current_user_authorizer]]. Both parameters are wired through FastAPI's `Depends` mechanism, meaning the framework resolves and injects them automatically when the function is used as a dependency in a route [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::check_article_modification_permissions]].

The function's sole logic is a permission check: it calls `check_user_can_modify_article` with the resolved article and user, and if that check returns a falsy value it raises an `HTTPException` with HTTP status `403 Forbidden`, signalling that the authenticated user is not the author of the article [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::check_article_modification_permissions]]. The function declares a return type of `None`, so callers that pass the check receive no value — the dependency is used purely for its side effect of gating access [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::check_article_modification_permissions]].

`get_article_by_slug_from_path` is an asynchronous FastAPI dependency function that retrieves a single article by its URL slug [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::get_article_by_slug_from_path]]. It accepts three injected parameters: `slug`, a path parameter validated to be at least one character long; `user`, an optionally authenticated [`User`](target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py) resolved via `get_current_user_authorizer(required=False)`, meaning unauthenticated callers are permitted [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::get_current_user_authorizer]]; and `articles_repo`, an [`ArticlesRepository`](target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py) instance injected through `get_repository` [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::get_repository]].

The function delegates the lookup to `articles_repo.get_article_by_slug`, passing both the slug and the (possibly absent) requesting user so that per-user context — such as whether the article is favourited — can be factored in [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::get_article_by_slug_from_path]]. If the repository signals that no matching article exists by raising `EntityDoesNotExist`, the function catches that exception and re-raises an `HTTPException` with a `404 Not Found` status code [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::get_article_by_slug_from_path]]. On success it returns the resolved [`Article`](target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py) object [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::get_article_by_slug_from_path]].

`get_articles_filters` is a dependency function that collects query-string filter parameters for listing articles and packages them into a single structured object [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::get_articles_filters]]. It accepts five optional inputs: `tag`, `author`, and `favorited` are plain `Optional[str]` values that default to `None`, while `limit` and `offset` are integers validated through FastAPI's `Query` helper — `limit` must be at least 1 and defaults to `DEFAULT_ARTICLES_LIMIT`, and `offset` must be at least 0 and defaults to `DEFAULT_ARTICLES_OFFSET` [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::get_articles_filters]]. The function constructs and returns an `ArticlesFilters` instance populated with all five values, which becomes the unified filter object consumed by the caller [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::get_articles_filters]]. Because every parameter has a default, no argument is required; a caller that provides none will receive a default-paged, unfiltered result set [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py]]. The use of `Query` on `limit` and `offset` signals that this function is designed to be injected as a FastAPI dependency, so the framework will parse and validate those fields directly from the HTTP query string before the function is invoked [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::get_articles_filters]].

This module is a collection of FastAPI dependency functions that handle article-related concerns — filtering, lookup, and access control — so that route handlers can declare these behaviours declaratively rather than repeating the logic inline [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py]].

[`get_articles_filters`](target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::get_articles_filters) is the simplest of the three: it gathers the query-string parameters used when listing articles and bundles them into a single `ArticlesFilters` object [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::get_articles_filters]]. It accepts optional `tag`, `author`, and `favorited` strings alongside integer `limit` and `offset` values that are validated through FastAPI's `Query` helper, ensuring `limit` is at least 1 and `offset` is at least 0 [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::get_articles_filters]]. Because every parameter carries a default, a caller that supplies none receives a default-paged, unfiltered result [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::get_articles_filters]].

[`get_article_by_slug_from_path`](target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::get_article_by_slug_from_path) is an asynchronous dependency that resolves a single `Article` from the URL slug [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::get_article_by_slug_from_path]]. It injects three values: the `slug` path parameter (validated to be at least one character), an optionally authenticated `User` via `get_current_user_authorizer(required=False)` so that unauthenticated callers are still permitted, and an `ArticlesRepository` instance for the database lookup [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::get_article_by_slug_from_path]]. Both the slug and the possibly-absent user are forwarded to the repository so that per-user context such as favourite status can be taken into account [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::get_article_by_slug_from_path]]. If the repository raises `EntityDoesNotExist`, the function catches it and re-raises an `HTTPException` with a `404 Not Found` status, translating a database-layer signal into a proper HTTP response [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::get_article_by_slug_from_path]].

[`check_article_modification_permissions`](target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::check_article_modification_permissions) builds directly on `get_article_by_slug_from_path`: it injects the already-resolved `Article` from that dependency alongside a now-required authenticated `User`, then calls `check_user_can_modify_article` to verify authorship [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::check_article_modification_permissions]]. If the check fails, it raises an `HTTPException` with a `403 Forbidden` status; if it passes, the function returns `None`, making it a pure gate that is used only for its side effect of blocking unauthorised requests [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::check_article_modification_permissions]]. The three functions therefore form a natural layering: the filter dependency feeds listing routes, the slug-lookup dependency feeds any route that targets a specific article, and the permission dependency composes on top of the lookup to guard write operations [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py]].

`__call__` is an asynchronous method on the [`RWAPIKeyHeader`](target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::RWAPIKeyHeader) class that acts as the callable entry point for the API key header dependency [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::RWAPIKeyHeader::__call__]]. It accepts a Starlette `Request` object and returns an `Optional[str]`, which will be the extracted API key value if one is present [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::RWAPIKeyHeader::__call__]].

The method delegates its core extraction logic to the parent class by awaiting `super().__call__(request)` [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::RWAPIKeyHeader::__call__]]. If the parent raises a `StarletteHTTPException` — for example, when no API key header is found — this method catches it and re-raises a FastAPI `HTTPException` using the same status code but substituting the detail message with the application-level `strings.AUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED` constant [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::RWAPIKeyHeader::__call__]]. This translation ensures that authentication failures surface a consistent, application-defined error message rather than the raw Starlette default [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::RWAPIKeyHeader::__call__]]. The `# noqa: WPS610` comment suppresses a linter warning on the `__call__` definition itself, consistent with the project's pattern of suppressing specific WPS rules for FastAPI dependency injection patterns [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::RWAPIKeyHeader::__call__]].

`RWAPIKeyHeader` is a class defined in [`target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py`](target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py) that extends FastAPI's `APIKeyHeader` security utility [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::RWAPIKeyHeader]]. It is not a Pydantic model; it is a dependency class whose single responsibility is to extract an API key from incoming request headers while enforcing an application-defined authentication error message [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::RWAPIKeyHeader]]. The class declares no fields of its own and inherits its header-extraction configuration directly from `APIKeyHeader` [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::RWAPIKeyHeader]].

The class exposes one method, `__call__`, which makes instances of `RWAPIKeyHeader` usable as FastAPI dependency callables [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::RWAPIKeyHeader::__call__]]. It accepts a Starlette `Request` object and returns an `Optional[str]` representing the extracted API key value when one is present [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::RWAPIKeyHeader::__call__]]. The actual extraction logic is delegated entirely to the parent class via `super().__call__(request)` [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::RWAPIKeyHeader::__call__]]. When the parent raises a `StarletteHTTPException` — for instance, because no API key header was found — `__call__` catches it and re-raises a FastAPI `HTTPException` using the same status code but replacing the detail with the `strings.AUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED` constant [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::RWAPIKeyHeader::__call__]]. This translation ensures that all authentication failures surface a consistent, application-defined message rather than the raw Starlette default [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::RWAPIKeyHeader::__call__]].

`_get_authorization_header` is a FastAPI dependency function that extracts and validates a Bearer-style token from an incoming API key header, returning the raw token string if it is valid [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header]].

It accepts two injected parameters: `api_key`, a string pulled from the request's authorization header via `Security(RWAPIKeyHeader(name=HEADER_KEY))`, and `settings`, the application configuration object supplied by `Depends(get_app_settings)` [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header]] [[target/app/core/config.py::get_app_settings]].

The function first attempts to split `api_key` on a single space, expecting exactly two parts — a prefix and a token — by calling `api_key.split(" ")` [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header]]. If the split produces any number of parts other than two (raising a `ValueError`), it immediately raises an `HTTPException` with status `403 Forbidden` [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header]]. It then checks whether the extracted prefix matches `settings.jwt_token_prefix`; if not, it raises a second `HTTPException`, also with status `403 Forbidden` and the same wrong-prefix detail message [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header]] [[target/app/core/config.py::get_app_settings]]. When both validations pass, the function returns the token portion of the header string as a plain `str` [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header]].

`_get_authorization_header_optional` is a FastAPI dependency function that attempts to extract and validate an authorization header, but tolerates its absence rather than failing [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header_optional]].

It accepts two injected parameters: an optional `authorization` string extracted from the request via `Security(RWAPIKeyHeader(..., auto_error=False))`, which suppresses automatic errors when the header is missing, and an `AppSettings` instance supplied by `Depends(get_app_settings)` [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header_optional]] [[target/app/core/config.py::get_app_settings]].

When `authorization` is present, the function delegates to `_get_authorization_header`, passing both the raw header value and the application settings, and returns whatever that call produces [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header_optional]]. When the header is absent, the function returns an empty string instead of raising an error, making it safe to use on endpoints that support both authenticated and unauthenticated access [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header_optional]].

The return type is `str` in both branches: either the processed header value from the delegate call, or `""` [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header_optional]]. No exceptions are raised directly by this function itself; any exception behaviour on a present-but-invalid header would be the responsibility of the inner `_get_authorization_header` call [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py]].

`_get_authorization_header_retriever` is a factory function that selects and returns one of two authorization-header retriever callables based on whether the header is required [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header_retriever]]. It accepts a single keyword-only argument, `required`, which defaults to `True` [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header_retriever]]. When `required` is `True`, the function returns `_get_authorization_header`; when `False`, it returns `_get_authorization_header_optional` [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header_retriever]]. The return type is annotated as `Callable`, with a `# type: ignore` comment suppressing the missing type-parameter warning [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header_retriever]]. This pattern allows callers to obtain the appropriate retriever for contexts where an Authorization header is either mandatory or optional, without duplicating the selection logic at each call site [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py]].

`_get_current_user` is an async FastAPI dependency that resolves the currently authenticated user from a bearer token [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_current_user]].

It accepts three injected parameters: a `UsersRepository` instance sourced via `get_repository` [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::get_repository]], a raw JWT string sourced via `_get_authorization_header_retriever` [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header_retriever]], and an `AppSettings` instance sourced via `get_app_settings` [[target/app/core/config.py::get_app_settings]]. All three are provided through FastAPI's `Depends` mechanism, meaning the framework resolves and injects them automatically at request time [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_current_user]].

The function first attempts to decode the token by calling `jwt.get_username_from_token`, passing the token and the application secret key retrieved via `settings.secret_key.get_secret_value()` [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_current_user]]. If that call raises a `ValueError` — indicating the token is malformed or its signature is invalid — the function raises an `HTTPException` with a `403 Forbidden` status and a malformed-payload detail message [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_current_user]].

If the username is successfully extracted, the function calls `users_repo.get_user_by_username` to look up the corresponding `User` record [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_current_user]]. Should that lookup raise an `EntityDoesNotExist` error — meaning no user matches the token's embedded username — the function again raises an `HTTPException` with `403 Forbidden` and the same malformed-payload detail, deliberately obscuring whether the failure was a bad token or a missing user [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_current_user]].

On the happy path, the function returns the resolved `User` object directly, making it suitable for use as an injected dependency in route handlers that require an authenticated user [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_current_user]].

`_get_current_user_optional` is an asynchronous dependency function that attempts to resolve the currently authenticated user, but treats authentication as optional rather than mandatory [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_current_user_optional]].

It accepts three injected parameters: a `UsersRepository` instance provided by `get_repository` [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::get_repository]], a `token` string retrieved by `_get_authorization_header_retriever` called with `required=False` — meaning no error is raised if the header is absent [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header_retriever]], and an `AppSettings` instance supplied by `get_app_settings` [[target/app/core/config.py::get_app_settings]].

When a token is present, the function delegates to the internal `_get_current_user` helper, passing along the repository, token, and settings, and returns whatever `User` object that call resolves [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_current_user_optional]]. When no token is present, the function returns `None` without any further processing, making the return type `Optional[User]` [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_current_user_optional]].

All three parameters are wired through FastAPI's `Depends` mechanism, so this function is designed to be used as a FastAPI dependency in route handlers that need to support both authenticated and unauthenticated requests [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_current_user_optional]].

`get_current_user_authorizer` is a factory function that selects and returns the appropriate user-authentication dependency based on whether authentication is mandatory for a given route [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::get_current_user_authorizer]]. It accepts a single keyword-only parameter, `required`, which is a `bool` defaulting to `True` [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::get_current_user_authorizer]]. Its return type is `Callable`, annotated with `# type: ignore` to suppress a typing limitation [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::get_current_user_authorizer]]. When `required` is `True`, it returns the `_get_current_user` dependency, which enforces authentication; when `required` is `False`, it returns `_get_current_user_optional`, which allows unauthenticated access [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::get_current_user_authorizer]]. The function itself performs no I/O or validation — it simply acts as a selector, making it easy to reuse authentication logic across routes that differ only in whether a logged-in user is strictly needed [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py]].

This module is the central authentication layer for the API, responsible for extracting bearer tokens from HTTP headers, validating them against application settings, and resolving them to domain `User` objects for injection into route handlers [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py]].

The foundation is `RWAPIKeyHeader`, a subclass of FastAPI's `APIKeyHeader` that overrides `__call__` to intercept any `StarletteHTTPException` thrown during header extraction and re-raise it as a FastAPI `HTTPException` carrying the application-defined `strings.AUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED` message [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::RWAPIKeyHeader]]. This ensures that every authentication failure surfaces a consistent error rather than a raw Starlette default, and it is the only class defined in the module [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::RWAPIKeyHeader]].

Header extraction is handled by a pair of complementary dependency functions. `_get_authorization_header` uses `RWAPIKeyHeader` in strict mode to pull the raw header value, splits it into a prefix and token, validates the prefix against `settings.jwt_token_prefix`, and returns the bare token string, raising a `403 Forbidden` exception for any malformed or mis-prefixed input [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header]]. Its counterpart, `_get_authorization_header_optional`, uses `RWAPIKeyHeader` with `auto_error=False` so that a missing header does not trigger an automatic error; when the header is present it delegates directly to `_get_authorization_header`, and when it is absent it returns an empty string instead of raising [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header_optional]]. The factory function `_get_authorization_header_retriever` encapsulates the choice between these two: when called with `required=True` (the default) it returns `_get_authorization_header`, and when called with `required=False` it returns `_get_authorization_header_optional`, avoiding repeated selection logic at every call site [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header_retriever]].

User resolution follows the same required/optional pattern one layer up. `_get_current_user` is an async dependency that takes the token produced by `_get_authorization_header_retriever`, decodes it with `jwt.get_username_from_token` against the application secret key, then fetches the matching record via `users_repo.get_user_by_username`; both a `ValueError` from the JWT decode and an `EntityDoesNotExist` from the repository lookup are caught and converted to a `403 Forbidden` response with a malformed-payload detail, deliberately obscuring which step failed [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_current_user]]. `_get_current_user_optional` wraps this by wiring `_get_authorization_header_retriever(required=False)` as its token source; when a token is present it delegates to `_get_current_user` and returns the resolved `User`, and when no token is present it returns `None`, making the return type `Optional[User]` [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_current_user_optional]].

The public surface of the module is a single factory, `get_current_user_authorizer`, which mirrors the structure of `_get_authorization_header_retriever` at the user level: passing `required=True` (the default) returns `_get_current_user`, while `required=False` returns `_get_current_user_optional` [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::get_current_user_authorizer]]. Route handlers throughout the application call this factory to obtain the correct authentication dependency for their needs, keeping the selection logic in one place [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::get_current_user_authorizer]].

`check_comment_modification_permissions` is a FastAPI dependency function that enforces write-access control on a comment, returning `None` on success and raising an `HTTP 403 Forbidden` exception if the requesting user is not authorised to modify it [[target/app/api/dependencies/comments.py::check_comment_modification_permissions]].

It accepts two injected parameters: a `Comment` object resolved by `get_comment_by_id_from_path`, which looks up the target comment from the request path, and a `User` object resolved by `get_current_user_authorizer()`, which identifies and authenticates the caller [[target/app/api/dependencies/comments.py::get_comment_by_id_from_path]] [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::get_current_user_authorizer]]. Both parameters are wired through FastAPI's `Depends` mechanism, so the framework resolves them automatically before the function body executes [[target/app/api/dependencies/comments.py::check_comment_modification_permissions]].

The body delegates the actual permission check to `check_user_can_modify_comment`, passing the resolved comment and user [[target/app/api/dependencies/comments.py::check_comment_modification_permissions]]. If that helper returns a falsy result, the function raises an `HTTPException` with status code `403` and an author-mismatch detail message, immediately halting the request [[target/app/api/dependencies/comments.py::check_comment_modification_permissions]].

`get_comment_by_id_from_path` is an async FastAPI dependency function that looks up a single comment by its numeric ID and returns it, raising a 404 if no matching comment is found [[target/app/api/dependencies/comments.py::get_comment_by_id_from_path]].

It accepts four injected parameters [[target/app/api/dependencies/comments.py]]. The `comment_id` is an integer extracted from the URL path, constrained to be greater than or equal to 1 via `Path(..., ge=1)` [[target/app/api/dependencies/comments.py::get_comment_by_id_from_path]]. The `article` parameter is resolved by delegating to `get_article_by_slug_from_path`, which fetches the article that the comment belongs to from the current request path [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::get_article_by_slug_from_path]]. The `user` parameter is resolved by `get_current_user_authorizer` called with `required=False`, meaning the caller does not need to be authenticated — an anonymous request is permitted and `user` will be `None` in that case [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::get_current_user_authorizer]]. The `comments_repo` parameter is a `CommentsRepository` instance injected through `get_repository`, providing the data-access layer for comments [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::get_repository]].

The function delegates the actual database lookup to `comments_repo.get_comment_by_id`, passing the resolved `comment_id`, `article`, and `user` [[target/app/api/dependencies/comments.py::get_comment_by_id_from_path]]. If the comment does not exist, `EntityDoesNotExist` is caught and re-raised as an `HTTPException` with HTTP status 404, so the caller receives a well-formed error response rather than an unhandled exception [[target/app/api/dependencies/comments.py::get_comment_by_id_from_path]].

This module provides two FastAPI dependency functions that together handle comment lookup and write-access control for the comments subsystem of the API [[target/app/api/dependencies/comments.py]].

`get_comment_by_id_from_path` is an async dependency that resolves a single comment from the current HTTP request [[target/app/api/dependencies/comments.py::get_comment_by_id_from_path]]. It extracts a numeric comment ID from the URL path (constrained to be at least 1), resolves the parent article via a delegated dependency, optionally identifies the requesting user (allowing unauthenticated callers by passing `required=False`), and obtains a `CommentsRepository` instance for data access — all through FastAPI's `Depends` mechanism [[target/app/api/dependencies/comments.py::get_comment_by_id_from_path]]. The actual database lookup is delegated to the repository's `get_comment_by_id` method; if the comment does not exist, the resulting `EntityDoesNotExist` exception is caught and re-raised as an `HTTPException` with HTTP 404, ensuring callers receive a well-formed error response rather than an unhandled exception [[target/app/api/dependencies/comments.py::get_comment_by_id_from_path]].

`check_comment_modification_permissions` builds directly on top of `get_comment_by_id_from_path` to enforce write-access control [[target/app/api/dependencies/comments.py::check_comment_modification_permissions]]. It injects the resolved `Comment` via `get_comment_by_id_from_path` and a fully authenticated `User` via `get_current_user_authorizer()` (authentication is required here, unlike in the lookup dependency) [[target/app/api/dependencies/comments.py::check_comment_modification_permissions]]. The body delegates the permission decision to `check_user_can_modify_comment`; if that helper returns a falsy value, the function raises an `HTTPException` with HTTP 403 and an author-mismatch detail message, immediately halting the request [[target/app/api/dependencies/comments.py::check_comment_modification_permissions]].

The two functions are designed to compose: route handlers that need both a resolved comment object and a guarantee that the caller may modify it can declare `check_comment_modification_permissions` as their sole dependency, which in turn pulls in `get_comment_by_id_from_path` automatically [[target/app/api/dependencies/comments.py::check_comment_modification_permissions]] [[target/app/api/dependencies/comments.py::get_comment_by_id_from_path]].

`_get_connection_from_pool` is an asynchronous generator function that borrows a single database connection from a connection pool and makes it available to the caller for the duration of a request [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::_get_connection_from_pool]]. It accepts one parameter, `pool`, which is a `Pool` instance injected automatically by FastAPI's dependency injection system via `Depends(_get_db_pool)`, meaning the pool itself is resolved by calling `_get_db_pool` before this function runs [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::_get_db_pool]] [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::_get_connection_from_pool]]. The function acquires a connection from that pool using `pool.acquire()` as an async context manager, then `yield`s the resulting `Connection` object to the dependent route or function [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::_get_connection_from_pool]]. Because it uses `yield`, FastAPI treats it as a dependency with cleanup: once the caller is finished, control returns here and the context manager releases the connection back to the pool automatically [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::_get_connection_from_pool]]. Its declared return type is `AsyncGenerator[Connection, None]`, confirming it produces exactly one `Connection` value and no final return value [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::_get_connection_from_pool]].

`list_articles` is an asynchronous route handler registered on `GET /api/articles` [[route:GET /api/articles]] that returns a paginated, filtered list of articles wrapped in a `ListOfArticlesInResponse` envelope [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::list_articles]].

It accepts three FastAPI-injected dependencies [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::list_articles]]. The first is `articles_filters`, an `ArticlesFilters` object resolved by `get_articles_filters` that carries the query-string filter criteria — `tag`, `author`, `favorited`, `limit`, and `offset` [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::get_articles_filters]]. The second is an optional `user`, resolved by `get_current_user_authorizer(required=False)`, meaning the endpoint is accessible to unauthenticated callers but will attach an authenticated `User` when a valid credential is present [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::get_current_user_authorizer]]. At runtime the function delegates to `articles_repo.filter_articles`, forwarding all five filter fields plus the optional `requested_user` so that per-user state (such as whether an article is favourited by the caller) can be computed inside the repository [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::list_articles]]. Each article returned from the repository is then converted to a serialisable form via `ArticleForResponse.from_orm` [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::list_articles]]. Finally, the handler constructs and returns a `ListOfArticlesInResponse` containing the converted list and its length as `articles_count` [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::list_articles]].

The decorator registers the handler with the FastAPI router under the name `articles:list-articles` and declares `ListOfArticlesInResponse` as the response model, so FastAPI will validate and serialise the return value automatically [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py]].

`retrieve_article_by_slug` is an asynchronous route handler that fetches and returns a single article by its URL slug [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::retrieve_article_by_slug]]. It is registered on the router as a GET endpoint at `/{slug}`, with the response serialized as an `ArticleInResponse` model and named `articles:get-article` [[route:GET /api/articles/{slug}]].

The function accepts a single parameter, `article`, which is resolved automatically by FastAPI's dependency injection system via `Depends(get_article_by_slug_from_path)` [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::get_article_by_slug_from_path]]. This means the slug is extracted from the URL path and the corresponding `Article` domain object is looked up before the handler body ever executes [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::retrieve_article_by_slug]].

The body converts the injected `Article` into a response-safe shape by calling `ArticleForResponse.from_orm(article)`, then wraps the result in an `ArticleInResponse` envelope, which is what the endpoint returns [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::retrieve_article_by_slug]]. Any failure to resolve the article — for example when the slug does not match a known record — would be handled inside the dependency rather than in this function itself [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::get_article_by_slug_from_path]].

`update_article_by_slug` is an asynchronous route handler registered on `PUT /{slug}` with the response model `ArticleInResponse` and the route name `articles:update-article` [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::update_article_by_slug]]. Before the handler body runs, FastAPI executes `check_article_modification_permissions` as a dependency declared directly on the route decorator, ensuring the caller is authorised to modify the article [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::check_article_modification_permissions]].

The function accepts three parameters [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::update_article_by_slug]]. `article_update` is an `ArticleInUpdate` object read from the request body, embedded under the JSON key `"article"` via FastAPI's `Body`. `current_article` is an `Article` instance resolved by `get_article_by_slug_from_path`, which looks up the existing article from the URL path segment [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::get_article_by_slug_from_path]]. `articles_repo` is an `ArticlesRepository` instance injected by `get_repository` [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::get_repository]].

Inside the body, if `article_update.title` is present a new slug is derived by calling `get_slug_for_article`; otherwise `slug` is left as `None` [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::update_article_by_slug]]. The handler then awaits `articles_repo.update_article`, passing the resolved `current_article`, the computed `slug`, and every field from `article_update` unpacked as keyword arguments [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::update_article_by_slug]]. Finally, the updated article is wrapped with `ArticleForResponse.from_orm` and returned inside an `ArticleInResponse` envelope, which FastAPI serialises as the HTTP response [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::update_article_by_slug]] [[route:PUT /api/articles/{slug}]].

This module defines the FastAPI router and all route handlers for the articles resource, covering the full set of CRUD operations that the articles API exposes [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py]].

A single `APIRouter` instance named `router` is declared at module level and serves as the mounting point for all five handlers [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py]].

[`list_articles()`](target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::list_articles) is registered on `GET ""` and returns a paginated, filtered collection of articles [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::list_articles]]. It accepts an `ArticlesFilters` object carrying `tag`, `author`, `favorited`, `limit`, and `offset` query parameters, an optional authenticated `User` (the endpoint is accessible without credentials), and an `ArticlesRepository` instance, all resolved through FastAPI dependency injection [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::list_articles]]. The handler forwards every filter field plus the optional caller identity to the repository, converts each returned article via `ArticleForResponse.from_orm`, and wraps the result in a `ListOfArticlesInResponse` envelope that includes the total count [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::list_articles]].

[`create_new_article()`](target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::create_new_article) is registered on `POST ""` and responds with HTTP 201 on success [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::create_new_article]]. It requires a fully authenticated user and an `ArticleInCreate` payload embedded in the request body under the key `"article"` [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::create_new_article]]. Before persisting anything, the handler derives a slug from the submitted title and checks whether that slug is already taken, raising an HTTP 400 exception if it is [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::create_new_article]]. If the slug is available, it delegates to the repository to persist the article and returns the result wrapped in an `ArticleInResponse` [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::create_new_article]].

[`retrieve_article_by_slug()`](target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::retrieve_article_by_slug) is registered on `GET /{slug}` and performs no database work of its own [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::retrieve_article_by_slug]]. The slug is extracted from the URL path and the corresponding `Article` domain object is fully resolved by the `get_article_by_slug_from_path` dependency before the handler body executes, so the body consists only of wrapping the injected article in an `ArticleInResponse` envelope [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::retrieve_article_by_slug]].

[`update_article_by_slug()`](target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::update_article_by_slug) is registered on `PUT /{slug}` and carries `check_article_modification_permissions` as a route-level dependency, so authorisation is enforced before the handler body runs [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::update_article_by_slug]]. It receives the existing article from the path via `get_article_by_slug_from_path` and an `ArticleInUpdate` payload from the request body [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::update_article_by_slug]]. When the update payload includes a new title, a fresh slug is derived; otherwise no slug change is requested [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::update_article_by_slug]]. The handler passes the current article, the computed slug, and all update fields unpacked as keyword arguments to the repository, then returns the updated article inside an `ArticleInResponse` [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::update_article_by_slug]].

[`delete_article_by_slug()`](target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::delete_article_by_slug) is registered on `DELETE /{slug}` and also declares `check_article_modification_permissions` as a route-level dependency, guaranteeing the caller is authorised before any deletion occurs [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::delete_article_by_slug]]. It resolves the target article from the path and an `ArticlesRepository` instance via injection, then issues a single awaited call to `articles_repo.delete_article`, after which it returns `None` and the framework sends an empty HTTP 204 response [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::delete_article_by_slug]].

The two slug-based mutation handlers (`update_article_by_slug` and `delete_article_by_slug`) share the same authorisation guard, while the two slug-based read handlers (`retrieve_article_by_slug` and the implicit lookup inside updates) share the same `get_article_by_slug_from_path` dependency for article resolution, making the permission and lookup logic consistent across the router without duplicating it inside the handler bodies [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::update_article_by_slug]] [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::delete_article_by_slug]] [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::retrieve_article_by_slug]].

The `articles` package is the self-contained routing layer for all article-related HTTP endpoints in the application, organised across three substantive modules and a package initialiser [[target/app/api/routes/articles]]. The `__init__.py` file is intentionally empty, existing only to mark the directory as a Python package [[target/app/api/routes/articles/__init__.py]].

The assembly point for the entire package is [`api.py`](target/app/api/routes/articles/api.py), which creates a single `APIRouter` and mounts the routers from both sibling modules under the `/articles` prefix, giving higher-level application wiring a single import to register every article endpoint at once [[target/app/api/routes/articles/api.py]].

The first of those two sibling modules, [`articles_resource.py`](target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py), owns the core CRUD surface of the articles API [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py]]. It exposes `GET ""` for paginated, optionally filtered article listings — accessible without authentication — and `POST ""` for creating a new article, where a slug is derived from the submitted title and rejected with HTTP 400 if it is already taken [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::list_articles]] [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::create_new_article]]. A `GET /{slug}` handler wraps a fully pre-resolved `Article` domain object in an `ArticleInResponse` envelope without performing any database work itself, because the lookup is handled entirely by the `get_article_by_slug_from_path` dependency [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::retrieve_article_by_slug]]. The `PUT /{slug}` and `DELETE /{slug}` handlers share a `check_article_modification_permissions` route-level dependency that enforces authorisation before their bodies execute, keeping permission logic out of the handler code and consistent across both mutations [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::update_article_by_slug]] [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::delete_article_by_slug]].

The second sibling module, [`articles_common.py`](target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py), covers the user feed and favouriting features [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py]]. `GET /feed` returns a paginated list of articles tailored to the authenticated caller, delegating the fetch entirely to the `ArticlesRepository` [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py::get_articles_for_user_feed]]. `POST /{slug}/favorite` and `DELETE /{slug}/favorite` are mirror-image handlers: the first persists a favouriting relationship and returns an `ArticleInResponse` with `favorited` set to `True` and `favorites_count` incremented, while the second removes it and returns the same envelope with `favorited` set to `False` and the count decremented; both raise HTTP 400 rather than allow a duplicate or a spurious removal [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py::mark_article_as_favorite]] [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py::remove_article_from_favorites]]. All three handlers in this module share the same structural pattern of depending on `get_current_user_authorizer` for authentication and `get_repository(ArticlesRepository)` for database access, keeping the route logic decoupled from both concerns [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py]].

The `login` function is an asynchronous route handler registered on `POST /api/users/login` via the `@router.post("/login", response_model=UserInResponse, name="auth:login")` decorator [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::login]] [[route:POST /api/users/login]]. It accepts three injected parameters: `user_login`, a `UserInLogin` value read from the request body under the `"user"` key; `users_repo`, a `UsersRepository` instance supplied by the `get_repository` dependency; and `settings`, an `AppSettings` instance supplied by `get_app_settings` [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::login]] [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::get_repository]] [[target/app/core/config.py::get_app_settings]].

The function begins by constructing an `HTTPException` with a 400 Bad Request status, which is reused for any failed login attempt so that callers cannot distinguish between a missing account and a wrong password [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::login]]. It then attempts to fetch the user record from the database by calling `users_repo.get_user_by_email` with the email supplied in the request body; if no matching record exists, an `EntityDoesNotExist` exception is caught and the generic `wrong_login_error` is raised in its place [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::login]]. If a record is found, `user.check_password` is called with the submitted password, and the same `wrong_login_error` is raised if the check fails [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::login]].

On success, a JWT is minted by calling `jwt.create_access_token_for_user`, passing the user object and the application secret key retrieved via `settings.secret_key.get_secret_value()` [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::login]] [[target/app/core/config.py::get_app_settings]]. The function returns a `UserInResponse` wrapping a `UserWithToken` that carries the user's username, email, bio, image, and the newly created token [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::login]].

`register` is an async function that handles new user registration, bound to the `POST /api/users` route with a 201 Created status code and a `UserInResponse` response model [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::register]] [[route:POST /api/users]].

It accepts three injected parameters: `user_create`, a `UserInCreate` object extracted from the request body under the key `"user"`; `users_repo`, a `UsersRepository` instance provided by the `get_repository` dependency; and `settings`, an `AppSettings` instance provided by `get_app_settings` [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::register]] [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::get_repository]] [[target/app/core/config.py::get_app_settings]].

Before creating any record, the function performs two uniqueness checks: it raises an `HTTPException` with HTTP 400 if the requested username is already taken, and raises a second `HTTPException` with HTTP 400 if the requested email address is already in use [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::register]].

If both checks pass, it persists the new user by calling `users_repo.create_user` with the fields unpacked from `user_create`, then generates a JWT access token by calling `jwt.create_access_token_for_user` using the newly created user and the application's secret key retrieved via `settings.secret_key.get_secret_value()` [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::register]] [[target/app/core/config.py::get_app_settings]].

Finally, it returns a `UserInResponse` wrapping a `UserWithToken` that carries the user's `username`, `email`, `bio`, `image`, and the freshly minted `token` [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::register]] [[route:POST /api/users]].

This module defines the authentication routes for the API, housing the two endpoints responsible for user login and registration [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py]]. It creates a single `APIRouter` instance that both handlers are attached to, and all imports — schemas, repository classes, JWT utilities, settings, and uniqueness-check helpers — are consolidated here to support those two operations [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py]].

The `login` function is an async route handler bound to `POST /login` that authenticates an existing user [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::login]]. It receives the caller's credentials from the request body, looks up the matching account via `users_repo.get_user_by_email`, and verifies the submitted password with `user.check_password` [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::login]]. To avoid leaking information about whether an account exists, both a missing account and a wrong password are surfaced through the same generic 400 Bad Request error [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::login]]. When credentials are valid, a JWT is minted with `jwt.create_access_token_for_user` using the application secret key, and the handler returns a `UserInResponse` wrapping a `UserWithToken` that carries the user's `username`, `email`, `bio`, `image`, and the new `token` [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::login]].

The `register` function is an async route handler bound to `POST ""` (the router's root) with a 201 Created status, and it creates a brand-new user account [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::register]]. Before persisting anything, it runs two uniqueness checks — one for the requested username and one for the requested email — and raises an HTTP 400 error immediately if either is already in use [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::register]]. If both checks pass, it calls `users_repo.create_user` to persist the record, then generates a JWT in exactly the same way `login` does, returning an identical `UserInResponse` / `UserWithToken` structure so that a successful registration delivers a ready-to-use token in the same shape as a successful login [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::register]].

The two handlers share a common output contract: both return `UserInResponse` wrapping `UserWithToken`, both generate the JWT through `jwt.create_access_token_for_user` with the secret sourced from `AppSettings`, and both depend on the same `UsersRepository` and `get_repository` injection pattern — making the module a self-contained boundary for all authentication concerns [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::login]] [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::register]].

`create_comment_for_article` is an asynchronous route handler registered on `POST /api/articles/{slug}/comments` that creates a new comment for a specific article and returns the saved comment wrapped in a response envelope [[target/app/api/routes/comments.py::create_comment_for_article]] [[route:POST /api/articles/{slug}/comments]].

The foundation is laid in [`base.py`](target/app/core/settings/base.py), which defines two tightly coupled types [[target/app/core/settings/base.py]]. `AppEnvTypes` is a plain Python `Enum` that enumerates the three valid deployment environments — `prod`, `dev`, and `test` — acting as a controlled vocabulary rather than a settings model [[target/app/core/settings/base.py::AppEnvTypes]]. `BaseAppSettings` extends Pydantic's `BaseSettings` and declares a single field, `app_env`, typed as `AppEnvTypes` and defaulting to `AppEnvTypes.prod`, so that every concrete settings instance is bound to one of those three environments and can draw its values from environment variables or a `.env` file [[target/app/core/settings/base.py::BaseAppSettings]].

Building on that foundation, [`app.py`](target/app/core/settings/app.py) defines `AppSettings`, which extends `BaseAppSettings` with the full set of fields the server needs to start [[target/app/core/settings/app.py::AppSettings]]. Fields are grouped by concern: seven describe the FastAPI application itself (including `title`, `version`, and `debug`), three govern database connectivity (`database_url`, `max_connection_count`, and `min_connection_count`), and four handle security and routing (`secret_key`, `api_prefix`, `jwt_token_prefix`, and `allowed_hosts`) [[target/app/core/settings/app.py::AppSettings]]. Its inner `Config` class sets `validate_assignment = True`, so Pydantic re-validates any field that is reassigned after construction, preventing silent misconfiguration [[target/app/core/settings/app.py::AppSettings]]. Beyond passive data storage, `AppSettings` actively participates in bootstrapping: the `fastapi_kwargs` property assembles the application metadata fields into the exact keyword-argument form expected by the FastAPI constructor, and the `configure_logging` method wires standard-library log records through an `InterceptHandler` into Loguru, registering `sys.stderr` as the sole sink at the configured level [[target/app/core/settings/app.py::AppSettings]].

The three remaining modules each extend `AppSettings` for a specific deployment context. `DevAppSettings` in [`development.py`](target/app/core/settings/development.py) enables debug mode, raises `logging_level` to `logging.DEBUG`, adjusts the application title, and directs the environment file loader to read from `.env` [[target/app/core/settings/development.py::DevAppSettings]]. `ProdAppSettings` in [`production.py`](target/app/core/settings/production.py) introduces no new fields and overrides only its inner `Config` class to redirect the loader to `prod.env`, with `app_env` inherited as `AppEnvTypes.prod` so any environment-branching logic unambiguously identifies it as production [[target/app/core/settings/production.py::ProdAppSettings]]. `TestAppSettings` in [`test.py`](target/app/core/settings/test.py) substitutes safe, deterministic values for test runs: debug is enabled, `secret_key` is hardcoded as `SecretStr("test_secret")`, both connection-pool bounds are fixed at `5`, and `database_url` is left without a default so it must be supplied explicitly at instantiation time, removing any accidental dependency on real infrastructure [[target/app/core/settings/test.py::TestAppSettings]].

The `core` package is the application's foundational layer, providing the configuration, lifecycle, and logging infrastructure on which the rest of the application depends [[target/app/core]]. Its [`__init__.py`](target/app/core/__init__.py) is intentionally empty, serving only to mark the directory as a Python package so that its submodules are importable by the rest of the application [[target/app/core/__init__.py]].

Configuration resolution is handled by [`config.py`](target/app/core/config.py), which acts as the single entry point for obtaining a settings object [[target/app/core/config.py]]. It maintains an `environments` dictionary that maps each of the three `AppEnvTypes` variants to the corresponding concrete settings class, and its [`get_app_settings()`](target/app/core/config.py) factory function reads the active environment from a baseline `BaseAppSettings` instance, looks up the correct class, and returns it as an `AppSettings` object [[target/app/core/config.py::get_app_settings]]. The `lru_cache` decorator ensures this resolution runs only once, so every caller across the application receives the same consistent instance [[target/app/core/config.py::get_app_settings]].

The concrete settings types themselves live in the [`settings`](target/app/core/settings) subpackage, which organises them into a layered hierarchy [[target/app/core/settings]]. The base of the hierarchy is `BaseAppSettings`, a Pydantic `BaseSettings` subclass that binds every instance to one of the three deployment environments via its `app_env` field [[target/app/core/settings/base.py::BaseAppSettings]]. `AppSettings` extends that base with the full complement of fields needed to start the server — covering application metadata, database connectivity, and security and routing — and adds active behaviour through its `fastapi_kwargs` property, which assembles those fields into the form the FastAPI constructor expects, and its `configure_logging` method, which routes standard-library log records through an `InterceptHandler` into Loguru [[target/app/core/settings/app.py::AppSettings]]. The three environment-specific subclasses each tailor that shared base: `DevAppSettings` enables debug mode and points the loader at `.env` [[target/app/core/settings/development.py::DevAppSettings]], `ProdAppSettings` redirects the loader to `prod.env` and relies on inherited defaults to identify itself as production [[target/app/core/settings/production.py::ProdAppSettings]], and `TestAppSettings` substitutes hardcoded, deterministic values to eliminate any accidental dependency on real infrastructure [[target/app/core/settings/test.py::TestAppSettings]].

The logging bridge lives in [`logging.py`](target/app/core/logging.py), which defines [`InterceptHandler`](target/app/core/logging.py), a minimal subclass of `logging.Handler` that intercepts standard-library log records and forwards them to Loguru [[target/app/core/logging.py::InterceptHandler]]. Its `emit` method resolves each record's level to a Loguru-native name where possible, falls back to the raw numeric level for non-standard levels, walks the call stack past the standard-library intermediary frames so that Loguru attributes the entry to the true originating call site, and finally dispatches with any accompanying exception information [[target/app/core/logging.py::InterceptHandler]].

Application lifecycle is managed by [`events.py`](target/app/core/events.py), which provides two factory functions that produce the async handlers FastAPI registers for startup and shutdown [[target/app/core/events.py]]. `create_start_app_handler` closes over the application instance and the settings object and returns a coroutine that calls `connect_to_db` before the first request is served [[target/app/core/events.py::create_start_app_handler]]. Its counterpart, `create_stop_app_handler`, returns a coroutine decorated with `@logger.catch` that calls `close_db_connection` on shutdown, ensuring that any teardown exception is captured and logged rather than silently lost [[target/app/core/events.py::create_stop_app_handler]]. Together the two functions form a symmetrical connection lifecycle that brackets the entire request-serving period of the application [[target/app/core/events.py::create_start_app_handler]] [[target/app/core/events.py::create_stop_app_handler]].

`connect_to_db` is an asynchronous function that establishes a PostgreSQL connection pool and attaches it to the FastAPI application's shared state [[target/app/db/events.py::connect_to_db]]. It accepts two parameters: `app`, a `FastAPI` instance, and `settings`, an `AppSettings` object that carries database configuration such as the database URL and connection pool bounds [[target/app/db/events.py::connect_to_db]].

When called, the function logs a "Connecting to PostgreSQL" message before attempting the connection, then invokes `asyncpg.create_pool` with the database URL (converted to a string via `str`) along with `min_size` and `max_size` drawn from `settings.min_connection_count` and `settings.max_connection_count` respectively [[target/app/db/events.py::connect_to_db]]. The resulting pool is stored on `app.state.pool`, making it accessible to the rest of the application for the duration of its lifetime [[target/app/db/events.py::connect_to_db]]. Once the pool is ready, a second log entry confirms that the connection has been established [[target/app/db/events.py::connect_to_db]].

The function returns `None` and declares no exceptions of its own, though failures in `asyncpg.create_pool` (for example an unreachable host or invalid credentials) would propagate to the caller [[target/app/db/events.py::connect_to_db]].

`target/app/db/events.py` is a module responsible for managing the lifecycle of the application's PostgreSQL connection pool [[target/app/db/events.py]]. It defines exactly two async functions — `connect_to_db` and `close_db_connection` — that are intended to be called at application startup and shutdown respectively [[target/app/db/events.py::connect_to_db]] [[target/app/db/events.py::close_db_connection]].

`connect_to_db` takes a `FastAPI` instance and an `AppSettings` object, uses `asyncpg.create_pool` to open a pool of PostgreSQL connections sized according to `settings.min_connection_count` and `settings.max_connection_count`, and stores the resulting pool on `app.state.pool` so that the rest of the application can reach it for the duration of its lifetime [[target/app/db/events.py::connect_to_db]]. Any failure inside `asyncpg.create_pool` — such as an unreachable host or invalid credentials — propagates directly to the caller, since the function catches no exceptions of its own [[target/app/db/events.py::connect_to_db]].

`close_db_connection` is the symmetric counterpart: it accepts only the `FastAPI` instance, retrieves the same `app.state.pool` that `connect_to_db` placed there, and awaits its `close()` method to tear the pool down cleanly [[target/app/db/events.py::close_db_connection]]. Both functions bracket their core operation with `loguru` log messages — one before and one after — so that connection events appear in the application's log output [[target/app/db/events.py::connect_to_db]] [[target/app/db/events.py::close_db_connection]]. Because both functions use `await`, they must be called from an asynchronous context, which aligns with FastAPI's async startup and shutdown event hooks [[target/app/db/events.py::connect_to_db]] [[target/app/db/events.py::close_db_connection]].

The module closes by instantiating each of the five table classes as module-level singletons (`users`, `articles`, `tags`, `articles_to_tags`, `favorites`), making them directly importable for use in query construction throughout the codebase [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py]].

[`target/app/services/security.py`](target/app/services/security.py) is a small password-security utility module that centralises hashing and verification behind a shared `passlib` context [[target/app/services/security.py]]. At module level it constructs a `CryptContext` instance named `pwd_context`, configured to use the `bcrypt` scheme, which the two hashing functions both delegate to [[target/app/services/security.py]].

`generate_salt` is a standalone helper that produces a fresh cryptographic salt and returns it as a plain UTF-8 string by calling `bcrypt.gensalt().decode()`; it takes no arguments and has no dependencies beyond the `bcrypt` library itself [[target/app/services/security.py::generate_salt]].

`get_password_hash` accepts a single plain-text `password` string and returns its hashed form by passing it directly to `pwd_context.hash`, with no branching or additional logic of its own [[target/app/services/security.py::get_password_hash]].

`verify_password` complements `get_password_hash` by accepting both a `plain_password` and a `hashed_password` and returning a boolean indicating whether they match, delegating the comparison entirely to `pwd_context.verify` [[target/app/services/security.py::verify_password]]. None of the three functions carry decorators, raise exceptions, or produce side effects [[target/app/services/security.py]].

The `services` package is the business-logic layer of the application, sitting between the HTTP routes and the data-access repositories and containing no route registrations or framework decorators of its own [[target/app/services]]. Its presence as a package is established by an empty initialiser file that contributes no definitions but makes all sibling modules importable under the `app.services` namespace [[target/app/services/__init__.py]].

Article-related logic is handled by [`articles.py`](target/app/services/articles.py), which provides three focused utilities [[target/app/services/articles.py]]. `check_article_exists` is an async helper that queries an `ArticlesRepository` by slug and translates an `EntityDoesNotExist` exception into a `False` return value rather than propagating it [[target/app/services/articles.py::check_article_exists]]. `get_slug_for_article` is a pure synchronous function that converts a plain title into a URL-friendly slug by delegating entirely to `slugify`, carrying no side effects [[target/app/services/articles.py::get_slug_for_article]]. `check_user_can_modify_article` enforces ownership by comparing the article's author username with the requesting user's username, returning `True` only when they match [[target/app/services/articles.py::check_user_can_modify_article]].

User-registration uniqueness checks live in [`authentication.py`](target/app/services/authentication.py), which exposes two closely parallel async functions [[target/app/services/authentication.py]]. `check_username_is_taken` queries the repository via `get_user_by_username` and returns `False` if `EntityDoesNotExist` is raised, `True` otherwise [[target/app/services/authentication.py::check_username_is_taken]]. `check_email_is_taken` follows the identical pattern but targets the email field through `get_user_by_email` [[target/app/services/authentication.py::check_email_is_taken]]. The two functions are designed to be called before a new account is persisted, not to perform the persistence themselves [[target/app/services/authentication.py]].

Comment ownership is handled by the single function `check_user_can_modify_comment` in [`comments.py`](target/app/services/comments.py), which compares the username stored on a comment's author against the supplied user's username and returns a plain boolean with no side effects or raised exceptions [[target/app/services/comments.py::check_user_can_modify_comment]].

JWT lifecycle management is the responsibility of [`jwt.py`](target/app/services/jwt.py), which fixes the token type, signing algorithm, and a one-week expiry lifetime in three module-level constants [[target/app/services/jwt.py]]. The low-level primitive `create_jwt_token` merges standard `exp` and `sub` claims into a copy of the caller's payload before encoding it, never mutating the original dictionary [[target/app/services/jwt.py::create_jwt_token]]. `create_access_token_for_user` is the application-facing entry point that serialises a `User` domain object into a `JWTUser` payload and delegates to `create_jwt_token` [[target/app/services/jwt.py::create_access_token_for_user]]. The inverse operation, `get_username_from_token`, decodes a raw token and returns the embedded username as a string, re-raising any cryptographic failure as a `ValueError` with the message `"unable to decode JWT token"` and any schema mismatch as a `ValueError` with the message `"malformed payload in token"` [[target/app/services/jwt.py::get_username_from_token]].

Password security is centralised in [`security.py`](target/app/services/security.py), which constructs a shared `passlib` `CryptContext` configured for `bcrypt` that all three of its functions delegate to [[target/app/services/security.py]]. `generate_salt` produces a fresh cryptographic salt and returns it as a plain UTF-8 string [[target/app/services/security.py::generate_salt]]. `get_password_hash` passes a plain-text password directly to `pwd_context.hash` and returns the result [[target/app/services/security.py::get_password_hash]], while `verify_password` accepts both a plain and a hashed password and returns a boolean match result via `pwd_context.verify`, with none of the three functions carrying decorators, raising exceptions, or producing side effects [[target/app/services/security.py::verify_password]] [[target/app/services/security.py]].

The `app` package is the top-level namespace for the entire FastAPI service, and its [`__init__.py`](target/app/__init__.py) is intentionally empty, existing solely to make the directory importable as a Python package [[target/app/__init__.py]]. All behaviour is distributed across seven submodules that each own a distinct layer of the application [[target/app]].

The entry point is [`main.py`](target/app/main.py), which defines the `get_application` factory and immediately invokes it to produce the module-level `app` instance that an ASGI server such as Uvicorn targets [[target/app/main.py]]. That factory wires together every other layer in sequence: it reads settings, configures logging, constructs the `FastAPI` instance, attaches CORS middleware, registers startup and shutdown lifecycle hooks, mounts the exception handlers for HTTP errors and validation failures, and finally attaches the top-level router under the path prefix declared in settings [[target/app/main.py::get_application]].

The foundational infrastructure lives in the `core` package, which provides the configuration resolution, logging bridge, and lifecycle event handlers on which the rest of the application depends [[target/app/core]]. Settings are resolved once through a cached factory that maps the active `AppEnvTypes` variant to the appropriate concrete class — development, production, or test — and that class exposes both a `fastapi_kwargs` property for the constructor and a `configure_logging` method that routes standard-library records through `InterceptHandler` into Loguru [[target/app/core/config.py::get_app_settings]]. The startup and shutdown handlers produced by `create_start_app_handler` and `create_stop_app_handler` bracket the entire request-serving period by calling into the database layer to open and close the connection pool [[target/app/core/events.py::create_start_app_handler]] [[target/app/core/events.py::create_stop_app_handler]].

Database connectivity and all data access are owned by the `db` package [[target/app/db]]. The `events` module manages an `asyncpg` pool stored on `app.state`, creating it at startup and tearing it down cleanly at shutdown [[target/app/db/events.py::connect_to_db]] [[target/app/db/events.py::close_db_connection]]. The `queries` sub-package anchors every SQL statement: `tables.py` exposes five pypika table singletons and a `Parameter` wrapper that emits asyncpg's `$n` placeholder syntax, while `queries.py` loads all `.sql` files via `aiosql` at import time into a single `queries` object that is the sole entry point for database operations [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py::TypedTable]] [[target/app/db/queries/queries.py]]. The repositories sub-package builds on top of those primitives: all five repository classes inherit connection management from `BaseRepository`, raise the sentinel `EntityDoesNotExist` on failed lookups, assemble domain objects in private hydration helpers, and compose one another on a shared connection rather than managing independent sessions [[target/app/db/repositories/base.py::BaseRepository]] [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository]] [[target/app/db/errors.py::EntityDoesNotExist]].

The `models` package defines every data shape the application works with, divided across three sub-packages [[target/app/models]]. Domain entities — `RWModel`, `User`, `UserInDB`, `Profile`, `Article`, and `Comment` — form the internal representation of the system's core objects, with `RWModel` providing camelCase aliasing and ISO 8601 datetime encoding for all descendants [[target/app/models/domain/rwmodel.py::RWModel]] [[target/app/models/domain/users.py::UserInDB]]. Schema types form the API boundary, validating incoming request bodies and serialising outgoing responses for every resource, with `RWSchema` adding ORM-mode hydration to the hierarchy [[target/app/models/schemas/rwschema.py::RWSchema]] [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ArticleForResponse]] [[target/app/models/schemas/users.py::UserWithToken]]. The shared mixins `DateTimeModelMixin` and `IDModelMixin` are composed freely into both layers wherever timestamps or integer identity are needed [[target/app/models/common.py::DateTimeModelMixin]] [[target/app/models/common.py::IDModelMixin]].

Business logic that does not belong in a route handler or a repository is isolated in the `services` package [[target/app/services]]. JWT creation and decoding, password hashing and verification, slug generation, ownership checks for articles and comments, and uniqueness pre-checks for usernames and emails are each handled by small, focused functions with no route decorators or framework dependencies [[target/app/services/jwt.py::create_access_token_for_user]] [[target/app/services/jwt.py::get_username_from_token]] [[target/app/services/security.py]] [[target/app/services/articles.py::check_user_can_modify_article]] [[target/app/services/authentication.py::check_username_is_taken]] [[target/app/services/authentication.py::check_email_is_taken]].

The HTTP surface is provided by the `api` package, which groups request wiring, error formatting, and routing into three sub-packages [[target/app/api]]. The `dependencies` sub-package translates headers, path parameters, and application state into typed domain objects that route handlers can declare directly, converting missing-entity signals into `404` responses and authorisation failures into `403` responses [[target/app/api/dependencies]]. The `errors` sub-package intercepts every `HTTPException` and validation failure and wraps them in a uniform `"errors"` envelope, also patching the OpenAPI schema so documentation matches the actual response shape [[target/app/api/errors/http_error.py]] [[target/app/api/errors/validation_error.py]]. The `routes` sub-package organises all endpoints into feature-specific modules assembled under one mountable router, covering authentication, user account management, profiles with follow and unfollow, articles with CRUD, pagination, feed, and favouriting, comment listing and ownership-gated deletion, and tag listing [[target/app/api/routes/api.py]] [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::register]] [[target/app/api/routes/profiles.py::follow_for_user]] [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py]] [[target/app/api/routes/comments.py::delete_comment_from_article]] [[target/app/api/routes/tags.py::get_all_tags]].

Finally, the `resources` package acts as a single registry of every string constant the API may return to a client, covering entity lookup results, ownership errors, authentication failures, and social-graph constraint violations, so that any part of the codebase reporting a problem to a caller imports a named constant rather than embedding text inline [[target/app/resources/strings.py]].

The application is a FastAPI service whose source code lives entirely within the `app` top-level package, which is intentionally empty at the root level and distributes all behaviour across seven focused submodules [[target/app]]. That shared class exposes a `fastapi_kwargs` property for the framework constructor and a `configure_logging` method that routes standard-library log records through `InterceptHandler` into Loguru [[target/app/core/settings]]. The three environment-specific subclasses tailor that base: `DevAppSettings` enables debug mode and reads from `.env`, `ProdAppSettings` redirects to `prod.env`, and `TestAppSettings` substitutes deterministic hardcoded values so test runs carry no dependency on real infrastructure [[target/app/core/settings]]. Application lifecycle is managed by two factory functions, `create_start_app_handler` and `create_stop_app_handler`, which produce the async coroutines FastAPI registers for startup and shutdown; together they bracket the request-serving period by calling into the database layer to open and close the connection pool [[target/app/core]].

Across the entire package, SQL lives in the `queries` module, connection management is inherited from `BaseRepository`, and repositories compose one another on a shared connection rather than managing independent sessions [[target/app/db/repositories]].

The `models` package defines every data shape the application works with, divided across shared mixins, a domain layer, and a schemas layer [[target/app/models]]. Two mixins in `common.py` are composed freely wherever needed: `DateTimeModelMixin` adds auto-populated `created_at` and `updated_at` timestamps, and `IDModelMixin` contributes an integer identity field aliased to `"id"` for JSON deserialisation [[target/app/models]]. All core entities inherit from it: `Profile` carries the public-facing view of a user, `User` holds application-facing account fields, and `UserInDB` extends `User` with database identity, timestamps, and the `change_password` and `check_password` methods that are the sole site for password hashing and verification [[target/app/models/domain]]. `Article` and `Comment` each compose `IDModelMixin`, `DateTimeModelMixin`, and `RWModel`, with both embedding `Profile` as the shared sub-model for author information [[target/app/models/domain]]. The schemas sub-package forms the API boundary, with `RWSchema` extending `RWModel` by adding `orm_mode = True` so schemas can be hydrated directly from database row objects [[target/app/models/schemas]]. Article schemas cover paginated listing filters, creation, partial updates, and both single and collection response envelopes; comment and user schemas follow the same envelope pattern at their respective scales; and `JWTMeta` and `JWTUser` separate generic token claims from application-specific user identity within a JWT payload [[target/app/models/schemas]].
